opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition comes down to what's happening in those very early iterations of training. At initialization, the network is in a really chaotic regime. The gradients are large, the weights move a lot, and small differences like the order of the data or the random seed can send you to quite different places in the loss landscape.

In the original lottery ticket experiments on smaller networks like MNIST models or small conv nets, you could rewind all the way back to initialization and the sparse subnetwork would still train to full accuracy. But when people scaled up to things like ResNets on ImageNet, that stopped working. The masked network reset to its initial weights just didn't recover the performance.

What Jonathan Frankle and colleagues found was that if you rewind not to iteration zero but to a point slightly into training, even a small fraction of the way through, the tickets start working again. One way I think about it is through their work on stability and linear mode connectivity. Very early in training, if you take two copies of the network and train them with different data orders, they end up in different basins, separated by a barrier in the loss. After a short amount of training, the network becomes stable: the two copies end up in the same linearly connected region. And that transition point lines up pretty closely with when rewinding starts to succeed.

So the story is that those first few epochs do a lot of important coarse work. They settle the network into a particular basin, and the weights pick up structure that isn't there at random initialization. Once you're past that point, the sparse subnetwork has enough of that structure baked in that it can follow a similar trajectory to the dense network. If you rewind all the way to initialization, you lose that, and the sparse network alone isn't robust enough to the noise of SGD to find its way back.

It also connects to some of what we looked at in our own work. The values and especially the signs of the weights carry a lot of information. Even a little bit of training can lock in a useful configuration that a purely random initialization doesn't have. So rewinding to a few epochs in is a way of keeping the information the network learned early, while still letting the subnetwork do most of the training itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions sensitivity to data order and random seed early in training, but does not say that a large dataset needs more exposure to provide a statistically representative picture of its distribution.

r002.rationale: It says early training moves the network into a basin and that, after a short time, training becomes stable, with copies reaching the same linearly connected region.

r003.rationale: It contrasts useful structure and information acquired after a few epochs with random initialization, and says this lets the sparse network follow a trajectory similar to the dense network.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find really interesting, and I'll be upfront that my understanding here is partly intuition rather than a settled result.

So the original lottery ticket work resets the winning ticket back to its initialization at step zero, and that works beautifully on small networks like LeNet on MNIST or small conv nets on CIFAR. But when you scale up to things like ResNets on ImageNet, or deeper networks with higher learning rates, that stops working. The winning tickets you find don't train well from the original init. And what Frankle and Carlin found, and then dug into more with the stability work, is that if you instead rewind to, say, a few hundred or a few thousand iterations into training, suddenly the tickets work again.

The way I think about it is that very early in training, the network is kind of settling on a region of the loss landscape. There's this notion of linear mode connectivity in the later paper, where they look at whether two copies of a network trained from the same point, but with different data order and noise, end up in the same basin. At initialization, for the larger networks, they don't. The SGD noise is enough to push them into totally different places. But a little way into training, they become stable, meaning you can perturb them and they still converge to the same basin. So rewinding to that point means the sparse subnetwork is starting from a position where the outcome of training is already roughly determined, and the pruning mask you found is actually relevant to the solution it's going to reach.

I think there's a nice connection to the masking work I did, where we looked at what the mask is actually doing. One of the things we found is that a lot of what matters in a winning ticket is the sign of the weights, not the precise values, and that the mask itself is doing something like training, because it's effectively setting a bunch of weights to zero, which was often the direction they were heading anyway. So when you rewind to a later point, you're keeping a version of the weights whose signs and rough magnitudes are consistent with the mask you're applying. At step zero on a big network, the weights are basically random with respect to the mask, and the mask is encoding information about a trajectory that this particular init may not follow again, because of all that early instability.

The other piece is just that the learning rate and the early phase of training with warmup matter a lot. In the original scaled-up experiments, if you used a smaller learning rate or warmup, the tickets started working again from init. That suggests that the problem is that aggressive early training moves the network far away in a noisy way, and rewinding past that noisy phase is a way of skipping it. So in some sense rewinding is not fundamentally different from using warmup, it's just another way to get past the point where the network hasn't yet committed to anything.

What I'd love to see, and I don't think we fully have, is a cleaner account of what information is actually being stored in those early iterations. Is it mostly in the signs? Is it the scale of the weights in particular layers? That's the kind of question where I think the masking experiments give you a toolkit, but we haven't pushed it all the way to the ImageNet scale cases yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses early SGD noise and instability, but does not say that the earliest epochs provide too little exposure to form a representative picture of the data distribution.

r002.rationale: It says the network settles into a region early and becomes stable, so perturbations still lead to the same basin.

r003.rationale: It describes rewinding weights as starting from a position where the training outcome is roughly determined, with signs and magnitudes consistent with the eventual solution.

astra-6.text:
My intuition is that those first few epochs help put the network in a position where the sparse subnetwork can actually train. In the original lottery ticket setup, you find a mask by pruning a trained network, then reset the surviving weights to their initial values. But as you scale up, that sparse network can be much harder to optimize from initialization.

Rewinding to a little bit later lets you retain some of the progress made while the network was still dense. The weights have started to adapt to the data, and their relative scales and directions may be more favorable for training. So even though you’re only keeping a small amount of training, it can make a substantial difference.

I’d distinguish that intuition from a complete explanation, though. Rewinding shows that the early training period matters; it doesn’t by itself tell us exactly what changes during that period make the ticket trainable.

r001.rationale: It says early training lets the sparse subnetwork become trainable, but does not mention insufficient data exposure or forming a representative picture of the data-generating distribution.

r002.rationale: It describes weights becoming more favorable for training, but does not propose that entering a solution basin makes later training dynamics less erratic.

r003.rationale: It says the rewound weights have begun adapting to the data and their scales and directions may be more favorable, indicating they better reflect the eventual solution than initialization weights.

sol-6.1.text:
My intuition is that those first few epochs help establish the conditions that make a sparse network trainable. In the original lottery ticket setup, you prune a trained network and reset the surviving weights to their initial values. But as you scale to deeper networks, that sparse network can become much harder to optimize from initialization.

If you rewind to a little later in training, you retain some of that early adaptation—perhaps more suitable weight scales or a more stable direction for optimization. The network hasn’t learned the whole task at that point, but it’s moved into a region from which the sparse subnetwork can train successfully.

I’d distinguish that intuition from a complete explanation, though. Rewinding shows that this early period matters; it doesn’t by itself tell us exactly which changes during that period are responsible.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest that early epochs provide too little exposure to form a representative picture of the data distribution.

r002.rationale: It mentions a more stable optimization direction, but does not connect entering a solution basin to less erratic subsequent training dynamics.

r003.rationale: It describes early adaptation and a trainable region, but does not say that the later weights better reflect the eventual solution than initialization weights.
